title: The Stolen Blessing and Its Cost
summary: Isaac plans to bless Esau in secret, Rebekah and Jacob deceive him, God’s purpose stands, and the family breaks apart.
historicalContext: The scene unfolds in Isaac’s camp in the Negeb, probably near Beersheba, late in his life. Reckoning backward from Jacob’s age before Pharaoh (47:9), the birth of Joseph, and Jacob’s fourteen years of service for his wives, Jacob was about seventy-seven when he fled, which makes Isaac roughly 137 and blind, though he would live to 180 (35:28). In patriarchal households the father’s final words were weighty acts. The birthright carried leadership and a double share of the estate (Deuteronomy 21:17), while the spoken blessing, pronounced in faith before God, was treated as prophetic and could not be recalled. A shared meal often framed such solemn moments. Esau had already married two Hittite women of the land (26:34–35). Haran, where Rebekah’s brother Laban lived, lay in upper Mesopotamia, hundreds of miles to the north. The later history of Israel and Edom, Esau’s descendants, shows how far Isaac’s words reached.
literaryContext: Genesis 27 is the hinge of the Jacob story. It follows the sale of the birthright (25:29–34) and Isaac’s years among the Philistines (chapter 26), and it is framed by notices of Esau’s marriages outside the covenant (26:34–35; 28:6–9). The narrative moves in paired scenes: Isaac with Esau, Rebekah with Jacob, Isaac with Jacob, Isaac with Esau, Rebekah with Jacob, and finally Rebekah with Isaac. Key words bind it together: “bless” and “blessing” recur nearly thirty times, while “venison,” “savoury meat,” “voice,” “son,” and “brother” keep appetite and kinship in view. The senses of a blind father, touch, taste, smell, and hearing, carry the plot. The chapter launches a long pattern of deceiving and being deceived that runs through Laban’s substitution of Leah (29:25) to the sons’ use of Joseph’s bloodied coat (37:31–33). It leads directly into Jacob’s open blessing and departure (28:1–5) and his encounter with God at Bethel.
themes: God’s purpose standing through human failure
The blessing of Abraham passing to Jacob
Despising holy things and craving them too late

outline.title: Isaac’s Private Plan
outline.summary: Old and blind, Isaac sends Esau to hunt game so that he may bless him over a favorite meal.

outline.title: Rebekah’s Counterplan
outline.summary: Rebekah overhears, commands Jacob to impersonate his brother, and prepares the meal and the disguise.

outline.title: Jacob Deceives His Father
outline.summary: Through repeated lies Jacob overcomes Isaac’s doubts and receives the blessing of fruitfulness, dominion, and Abraham’s protection.

outline.title: Esau’s Bitter Cry
outline.summary: Esau returns too late; Isaac trembles, confirms Jacob’s blessing, and gives Esau a word of a harder lot.

outline.title: Hatred and Flight
outline.summary: Esau plots murder, Rebekah sends Jacob toward Haran, and she secures Isaac’s consent by pointing to Esau’s Hittite wives.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, that when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see, he called Esau his eldest son, and said unto him, My son: and he said unto him, Behold, here am I.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The chapter opens in decline. “When Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see” sets the conditions the whole plot will exploit. The chronology of Jacob’s later life places the scene late in Isaac’s years. Jacob told Pharaoh he was 130 (47:9); Joseph was then about thirty-nine, so Jacob was about ninety-one when Joseph was born, at the close of fourteen years of service for Leah and Rachel. Jacob therefore left home at about seventy-seven, and Isaac, sixty when the twins were born (25:26), was near 137. He would live to 180 (35:28). The man who feels death at the door still has more than four decades before him.

The failing eyes are literal, yet the narrator lets them carry a second weight. Isaac’s sight fades at the very time his spiritual perception is clouded. Before the twins were born the LORD had said, “the elder shall serve the younger” (25:23). Esau had since treated the birthright as worthless (25:34) and married two Hittite women who embittered his parents (26:34–35). Isaac still turns to the son he prefers. Elsewhere Scripture pairs dim eyes with dim discernment, as with Eli at Shiloh (1 Samuel 3:2; 4:15).

He calls “Esau his eldest son,” and the title reveals the frame of his thinking: rank by birth, rather than the purpose God had announced, governs his choice. Esau answers, “Behold, here am I,” the same reply Abraham gave when God called him to Moriah (22:1, 11) and Isaac himself spoke on the mountain path (22:7). There it expressed readiness to obey God. Here it opens a private conference between a father and his favorite that leaves God’s word out of the room. The family that once climbed Moriah together is dividing into camps.

wordNotes.term: וַתִּכְהֶיןָ עֵינָיו (vattikhena ʿenav) — his eyes were dim
wordNotes.explanation: The verb כָּהָה (kahah) means to grow faint or dull, and with eyes it describes sight weakened by age or sorrow. Moses at 120 is noted because his eye “was not dim,” and Eli’s eyes “began to wax dim” in old age. Here the word explains how a disguise could succeed, and the story lets Isaac’s physical dimness mirror his failure to see what God had already said.

wordNotes.term: הִנֵּנִי (hinneni) — here am I
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “behold me,” the ordinary reply of someone ready to listen and act. It is the answer of Abraham to God at Moriah and of Isaiah at his call. Its use between Isaac and Esau recalls those moments of surrender while introducing a scene where God’s will is being sidestepped.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Behold now, I am old, I know not the day of my death:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Behold now, I am old, I know not the day of my death.” Isaac speaks as a man putting his affairs in order. In the ancient household a father commonly delivered his last words and blessings when he believed the end was near; Jacob would later gather his sons for that purpose (49:1), and Moses would bless the tribes before his death (Deuteronomy 33:1). Isaac’s sense of urgency was mistaken by decades, yet the feeling is understandable. Ishmael, his older half brother, had died at 137 (25:17), and Isaac may have felt that his own time had come.

The statement carries an irony. A man who confesses he does not know the day of his death acts as though he knows how the blessing ought to go. Uncertainty about tomorrow could have driven him to seek the LORD and to gather the whole household. Instead it hurries him into a private arrangement. Scripture counsels a different response to life’s brevity: “So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom” (Psalm 90:12). Knowing that life is short should make a believer more careful to align his decisions with God’s revealed will, not more anxious to secure his own preferences before time runs out.

wordNotes.term: יוֹם מוֹתִי (yom moti) — the day of my death
wordNotes.explanation: An ordinary Hebrew way of speaking about the end of life as a fixed but unknown day. Genesis describes patriarchal deaths simply as breathing out life and being gathered to one’s people, the language of the grave and the family tomb. Isaac’s words reflect the common awareness that the timing of death lies beyond human knowledge.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow, and go out to the field, and take me some venison;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac’s instructions are specific: “take, I pray thee, thy weapons, thy quiver and thy bow, and go out to the field, and take me some venison.” Every element belongs to Esau’s world. He was “a cunning hunter, a man of the field,” and “Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison” (25:27–28). The request revives the appetite that shaped Isaac’s preference long before. The field is Esau’s domain, as the tent is Jacob’s.

Nothing in the errand is wrong in itself. Game from the hunt was lawful food, and a meal was a fitting way to mark a solemn occasion. What troubles the reader is the setting. The blessing of Abraham concerned God’s covenant, the land of promise, and the Seed through whom all nations would be blessed. Isaac ties its transmission to a hunt and a favorite dish. The son who once lay bound on the altar at Moriah now arranges the passing of the promise around his palate.

The word “venison” translates the general Hebrew term for game, any animal taken in hunting, not deer in particular. It recurs through the chapter alongside “savoury meat,” keeping food in front of the reader until the meal becomes the very instrument of deceit. Esau had sold his birthright for bread and lentil stew (25:33–34); now his father is ready to bestow the blessing over another dish. Hebrews holds up Esau’s trade as a warning against profane priorities (12:16), and here the father shares the son’s weakness.

wordNotes.term: צַיִד (tsayid) — venison
wordNotes.explanation: The noun means game, any creature taken by hunting. The written consonants here read צֵידָה, while the reading tradition gives צַיִד; the sense is the same. It shares its stem with the description of Esau as “a cunning hunter,” literally a man who knows game. Its frequent repetition in the chapter underlines how appetite has entered the transmission of the blessing.

wordNotes.term: כֵּלֶיךָ (kelekha) — thy weapons
wordNotes.explanation: כְּלִי (keli) is a broad word for an implement, vessel, or piece of equipment, and the context determines its sense. Here it means hunting gear, further defined as quiver and bow. The same word describes Jonathan’s “artillery” handed to his lad and, in Jacob’s last words, the “instruments of cruelty” of Simeon and Levi.

verses.bibleText: And make me savoury meat, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat; that my soul may bless thee before I die.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac asks for “savoury meat, such as I love.” The verb is the ordinary word for love, the same used when the narrator said Isaac loved Esau (25:28) and loved Rebekah (24:67). Affection for the son and craving for the dish have become entangled. The purpose of the meal comes last: “that my soul may bless thee before I die.”

“My soul” is the common Hebrew idiom for the self. The word נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh) denotes the living person, the whole of who one is, so the phrase means “that I myself may bless thee,” with full intent and vigor. It lends no support to the idea of an immortal soul housed in the body. Isaac speaks as a whole living being who expects to die and return to the dust (3:19), and the blessing he intends is the act of a living man before death, not something carried beyond it.

A patriarchal blessing was more than a kindly wish. Spoken in faith, it became a prophetic declaration that God would honor, which is why Hebrews remembers that “by faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come” (11:20). Isaac knows this, which makes the private arrangement so serious. A pronouncement of such weight would naturally be given before the household, as Jacob later blessed all his sons together (49:1–28). By confining it to Esau and a meal, Isaac seems aware that he is moving against what God had revealed at the twins’ birth. He sets his preference against the oracle of 25:23 without consulting Rebekah, without calling Jacob, and without inquiring of the LORD.

Here the chapter’s moral pattern begins. Every member of the family will act on private judgment, and none will wait for God. Isaac goes first, and his choice creates the crisis that tempts the others. Those who carry spiritual responsibility in a home teach by example; when they bend God’s revealed will to personal fondness, they invite others to answer one wrong with another.

wordNotes.term: מַטְעַמִּים (matʿammim) — savoury meat
wordNotes.explanation: From the verb “to taste,” the word means tasty dishes or delicacies. Proverbs uses a related form for the “dainties” of a ruler’s table and warns against desiring them, since such food can be deceitful. The chapter repeats the term to keep Isaac’s appetite before the reader.

wordNotes.term: תְּבָרֶכְךָ נַפְשִׁי (tevarekhekha nafshi) — that my soul may bless thee
wordNotes.explanation: נֶפֶשׁ (nephesh) here stands for the person himself, as in “Bless the LORD, O my soul.” The idiom expresses wholehearted personal action. Genesis 2:7 shows that the human being became a living nephesh when God breathed life into dust; the word describes the living person, not a separable immortal part.

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah heard when Isaac spake to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Rebekah heard when Isaac spake to Esau his son.” The Hebrew participle pictures her listening while Isaac was speaking, close enough to catch every word. The narrator calls Esau “his son,” Isaac’s, and in the next verse Jacob will be “her son.” The division in the family is written into the grammar. The favoritism planted in 25:28 has grown into two camps.

Rebekah had reason for alarm. She had received the oracle about the twins directly from the LORD when she went to inquire of Him (25:22–23), and now she could see her husband preparing to set it aside. The danger was real; the question was what faith should do about it. She might have spoken openly to Isaac, reminded him of God’s word, or carried the matter to the LORD as she had once done when the children struggled within her. Instead she concluded that God’s purpose needed her ingenuity to survive. In her reasoning a deception that served the divine plan could be excused.

That line of thought is one of the oldest temptations: a worthy goal is supposed to sanctify crooked means. Isaiah pronounces woe on those who “call evil good, and good evil” (Isaiah 5:20), and Paul flatly rejects the slogan “Let us do evil, that good may come” (Romans 3:8). God had no need of Rebekah’s scheme. The One who later turned a hired prophet’s intended curse into blessing (Numbers 23:20) could have guarded His purpose for Jacob without a single lie.

Meanwhile “Esau went to the field to hunt for venison, and to bring it.” The two errands now run side by side, one in the open country and one in the tent, and the reader waits to see which will reach Isaac first.

wordNotes.term: וְרִבְקָה שֹׁמַעַת (veRivqah shomaʿat) — and Rebekah heard
wordNotes.explanation: The participle describes ongoing action: Rebekah was listening as Isaac spoke, much as Sarah listened at the tent door when the visitors spoke of Isaac’s birth. The verb שָׁמַע (shamaʿ) can mean both to hear and to obey, and the chapter plays on that range; having heard, Rebekah will command Jacob to “obey my voice.”

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah spake unto Jacob her son, saying, Behold, I heard thy father speak unto Esau thy brother, saying,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah goes straight to “Jacob her son.” She reports what she overheard, naming Isaac as “thy father” and Esau as “thy brother.” Every relationship she mentions will be injured by the plan she is about to propose: a father will be misled and a brother defrauded. The vocabulary of kinship sits uneasily beside the scheme.

The verse marks Rebekah as the one who sets events in motion. Jacob had already shown himself eager for the birthright (25:31), yet here he does not devise the plot. Still, the narrative will not excuse him. He listens, he objects only on practical grounds, and he carries out every step. Responsibility in this chapter is shared among the four, even though it is not distributed evenly.

The household of Abraham offers a telling comparison. When Sarah urged a course concerning Hagar and Ishmael, she spoke to her husband directly (16:2; 21:10), and God then guided Abraham’s response (21:12). In Isaac’s tent husband and wife no longer speak to one another about the matter that most concerns them both. Isaac’s secrecy invites Rebekah’s, and a family that should have sought God together now works in rival directions.

wordNotes.term: אָחִיךָ (ʾakhikha) — thy brother
wordNotes.explanation: “Brother” recurs throughout the chapter, and each use sharpens the wrong being done to a sibling. The word recalls the first brothers, when Cain asked, “Am I my brother’s keeper?” and the chapter will end with Esau resolving to kill his brother. John points to Cain as the pattern of hatred toward a brother.

verses.bibleText: Bring me venison, and make me savoury meat, that I may eat, and bless thee before the LORD before my death.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah quotes Isaac’s words to Esau with one striking addition. Isaac had said, “that my soul may bless thee before I die” (v. 4). In her report the blessing will be given “before the LORD before my death.” Whether she supplies the phrase or repeats words the narrator earlier abbreviated, her version brings out what was at stake. This was no ordinary farewell. A blessing pronounced before the LORD would be spoken under God’s own witness, and once given it could not be recalled.

The phrase serves her purpose. By stressing the sacred weight of the moment she persuades Jacob that doing nothing would be disastrous. Yet the same words judge her. If the blessing is to be spoken in the LORD’s presence, then the LORD governs it, and He had already declared His will concerning Jacob. A blessing given “before the LORD” could hardly be captured against His purpose, and it did not require a lie to reach the heir He had named.

Israel’s faith understood that words spoken in God’s name carried weight. The priests would later place the LORD’s name upon the people through the Aaronic blessing (Numbers 6:23–27), and the patriarchal blessings functioned in a similar way, as declarations God would honor. That is why Isaac will later say, “yea, and he shall be blessed” (v. 33). Rebekah’s reverence for the moment is sound; the method she is about to choose contradicts it. It is possible to speak rightly of God’s presence while acting as though He were absent, and Proverbs reminds us that His eyes are in every place (15:3).

wordNotes.term: לִפְנֵי יְהוָה (lifne YHWH) — before the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “to the face of the LORD,” the phrase describes an act done in His presence and under His witness. Abraham stood “before the LORD” in intercession, and David and Jonathan made their covenant “before the LORD.” Applied to the blessing, it marks Isaac’s words as a solemn act under God’s oversight rather than a private family matter.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore, my son, obey my voice according to that which I command thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now therefore, my son, obey my voice according to that which I command thee.” Rebekah speaks in the vocabulary of authority. “Obey my voice” is the very expression God used of Abraham’s faithfulness: “because thou hast obeyed my voice” (22:18; 26:5). “Command” is the verb used both of divine charges and of a parent’s instruction. Rebekah casts herself as the one whose word must be followed without discussion.

Parental authority is real and honored in Scripture. The fifth commandment calls children to honor father and mother (Exodus 20:12), and the principle was understood long before Sinai. Yet no human authority may require what God forbids. Jacob’s duty to his mother did not extend to lying to his father; when a parent’s command collides with God’s, the higher obligation governs (Acts 5:29). Paul frames a child’s obedience as obedience “in the Lord” (Ephesians 6:1), which sets its limits as well as its warrant.

Rebekah uses this phrase three times in the chapter (vv. 8, 13, 43). Each time it drives Jacob along a path she has chosen: first into deception, then past his hesitation, and finally into flight. Her last recorded words to her son will be one more command to obey her voice. The deception that begins here ends with her sending away the son she loves, and the narrative records no later meeting between them.

wordNotes.term: שְׁמַע בְּקֹלִי (shemaʿ beqoli) — obey my voice
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “hear in my voice,” the Hebrew idiom for obedience: listening that issues in doing. It is the language of Abraham’s obedience to God and of God’s call to Israel at Sinai. On Rebekah’s lips it claims for her own plan the kind of compliance owed to God’s word.

verses.bibleText: Go now to the flock, and fetch me from thence two good kids of the goats; and I will make them savoury meat for thy father, such as he loveth:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The plan is concrete: “Go now to the flock, and fetch me from thence two good kids of the goats.” Rebekah is confident that meat from the household flock, well seasoned, can pass for wild game. She knows her husband’s taste, “such as he loveth.” Familiarity with his preferences, which should serve love, now serves deceit.

Two kids would provide far more than one man could eat. Perhaps she wanted the choicest cuts from each, or perhaps she was already thinking of their skins (v. 16). Either way, the flock near the tent replaces the open field. Jacob, “a plain man, dwelling in tents” (25:27), does not need to hunt; the means lie close at hand. The ease of the substitution is part of the warning. The deceptions that cause the most harm often require the least effort.

Goats will return in Jacob’s story with painful symmetry. Years later his own sons will kill a kid of the goats, dip Joseph’s coat in its blood, and bring it to their father, who will be misled by what he sees and handles (37:31–33). Judah will pledge a kid of the goats to Tamar and be exposed by the tokens he surrendered (38:17–26). The man who used a goat to deceive his father will be deceived by a goat in his own old age. Scripture records the pattern without comment and lets the principle of Galatians 6:7 speak through the events: “whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.”

wordNotes.term: גְּדָיֵי עִזִּים טֹבִים (gedaye ʿizzim tovim) — good kids of the goats
wordNotes.explanation: Young goats, here described as “good,” meaning choice animals suitable for a fine meal. The same animal reappears in the bloodied coat brought to Jacob and in Judah’s pledge to Tamar, linking this scene to later deceptions within the family.

verses.bibleText: And thou shalt bring it to thy father, that he may eat, and that he may bless thee before his death.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah finishes her instructions: “thou shalt bring it to thy father, that he may eat, and that he may bless thee before his death.” She makes no attempt to soften the purpose. Jacob is to take Esau’s place at the meal and so receive what Isaac intended for Esau.

She repeats the phrase “before his death,” keeping the pressure of time before Jacob’s eyes. To her the moment seems unrepeatable. Faith may feel the same urgency and still choose another path. David, already anointed, twice refused to seize the kingdom by striking Saul when opportunity lay in his hands (1 Samuel 24:6; 26:9–11). The promise God had given to Rebekah did not hang on her timing, and the psalmist’s counsel applies: “Rest in the LORD, and wait patiently for him” (Psalm 37:7).

wordNotes.term: בַּעֲבֻר אֲשֶׁר יְבָרֶכְךָ (baʿavur asher yevarekhekha) — that he may bless thee
wordNotes.explanation: The conjunction expresses purpose: everything in the plan is subordinated to securing the blessing. The verb בָּרַךְ (barakh), to bless, is the key word of the chapter, appearing with its noun again and again. It reaches back to God’s first blessing on humanity and His promise to make Abraham a blessing.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob raises an objection: “Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man.” The difference had been obvious from birth, when Esau came out “red, all over like an hairy garment” (25:25). Jacob knows that a blind father will rely on touch.

What he leaves unsaid is revealing. He raises no question of right or wrong. He does not say, “I cannot lie to my father,” or “Let us wait for the LORD who promised.” His only worry is exposure. Conscience can stay quiet so long as discovery seems unlikely. Joseph, facing a far stronger temptation in Potiphar’s house, would ask the question Jacob never asks: “how then can I do this great wickedness, and sin against God?” (39:9).

The Hebrew word for “smooth” is also used of flattering, slippery speech (Proverbs 5:3; Psalm 12:2). The narrator does not draw the connection, but a reader may sense that the smoothness of Jacob’s skin will be matched by the smoothness of his tongue in the scene to come. The word for “hairy,” saʿir, sounds like Seir, the hill country that would become the home of Esau’s descendants (32:3; 36:8). Even the brothers’ bodies anticipate their national futures.

wordNotes.term: חָלָק (khalaq) — smooth
wordNotes.explanation: The adjective describes a hairless surface here, but the same word family is used for smooth stones in a brook and for flattering lips and smooth words. The physical description fits Jacob’s skin, while its wider use hints at the slippery speech he is about to employ.

wordNotes.term: שָׂעִר (saʿir) — hairy
wordNotes.explanation: The word recalls Esau’s birth, when he emerged like a hairy garment, and it echoes Seir, the mountainous region where Esau later settled. Genesis often lets names and descriptions anticipate the destiny of a person or people.

verses.bibleText: My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“My father peradventure will feel me, and I shall seem to him as a deceiver; and I shall bring a curse upon me, and not a blessing.” Jacob pictures the scene clearly: his father’s hands on his arms, the shock of recognition, and the blessing turned to a curse. He understands that a patriarch’s spoken word carried real weight before God.

“Deceiver” translates a rare Hebrew form meaning one who mocks or makes sport of another. The only other place the verb appears is 2 Chronicles 36:16, where Judah “misused” God’s prophets, treating them with derision. Jacob grasps that what he is about to do would make his blind father the victim of a cruel trick. The Law would later forbid putting a stumblingblock before the blind and pronounce a curse on anyone who “maketh the blind to wander out of the way” (Leviticus 19:14; Deuteronomy 27:18). Jacob’s instinct that such an act invites a curse is correct.

Yet he frames the danger entirely in terms of how he will “seem.” He is anxious about being seen as a deceiver, not about being one. The contrast between seeming and being runs through the chapter. Jacob will seem to be Esau, goat will seem to be game, and the blessing will seem lost to Esau forever. God sees through every appearance: “man looketh on the outward appearance, but the LORD looketh on the heart” (1 Samuel 16:7).

Paul distinguishes worldly sorrow, which regrets consequences, from godly sorrow, which leads to repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10). Jacob’s hesitation belongs to the first kind. It will take years of hardship, Laban’s own deceptions, and a night of wrestling at the Jabbok before the supplanter becomes Israel (32:28). Grace takes hold of people where they are, and it does not leave them there.

wordNotes.term: כִּמְתַעְתֵּעַ (kimtaʿteaʿ) — as a deceiver
wordNotes.explanation: The verb behind this form means to mock, to trifle with, or to make sport of someone. It occurs elsewhere only in 2 Chronicles 36:16, of Judah’s scornful treatment of the prophets. Jacob recognizes that impersonating Esau would make a mockery of his blind father, the kind of cruelty the Law later forbade.

wordNotes.term: קְלָלָה (qelalah) — a curse
wordNotes.explanation: The noun is the opposite of בְּרָכָה (berakhah), blessing, and the two are often set side by side as alternatives. Moses later placed blessing and curse before Israel as the outcomes of obedience and disobedience. Jacob fears that his father’s words, instead of conveying favor, will pronounce misfortune upon him.

verses.bibleText: And his mother said unto him, Upon me be thy curse, my son: only obey my voice, and go fetch me them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah meets Jacob’s fear with a vow: “Upon me be thy curse, my son: only obey my voice, and go fetch me them.” She is so certain of her course that she offers to absorb whatever consequence may fall. The words sound brave, even sacrificial. They are also rash. No one can shift moral guilt by declaring it so, and Rebekah has no power to redirect a curse from one person to another.

Her confidence probably rested on the oracle. Knowing that God had designated Jacob, she may have reasoned that no curse could land where God intended blessing. In one sense she was right: the curse Jacob feared never came from Isaac’s lips. Yet she was wrong to suppose that an end she knew to be God’s would shelter the means she had chosen. The consequences arrived by other roads. Within days she would be urging Jacob to run for his life, and Genesis tells of no reunion. Her death passes without notice, though the burial of her nurse Deborah is recorded (35:8), and her own burial in the family tomb surfaces only in Jacob’s last words (49:31).

“Upon me be thy curse” finds a dark echo in the crowd before Pilate: “His blood be on us, and on our children” (Matthew 27:25). Both sayings come from confident self-will, inviting consequences the speakers did not understand. Both also stand in contrast with the one place in Scripture where a curse is truly carried by another. “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Galatians 3:13). Rebekah’s offer was presumption. His was substitution, freely chosen in obedience to the Father and effective because He was without sin.

Her closing insistence, “only obey my voice,” ends the discussion. She leaves Jacob no room to reconsider, and he does not ask for any.

wordNotes.term: עָלַי קִלְלָתְךָ (ʿalay qilelatekha) — upon me be thy curse
wordNotes.explanation: A formula of self-imposed liability: “on me be the curse meant for you.” Such words appear elsewhere in rash or defiant oaths, most memorably in the crowd’s cry at Jesus’ trial. The only true bearing of another’s curse is Christ’s, who became a curse by hanging on the tree, in keeping with the law’s own words about one hanged.

verses.bibleText: And he went, and fetched, and brought them to his mother: and his mother made savoury meat, such as his father loved.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he went, and fetched, and brought them to his mother.” Three quick verbs register Jacob’s compliance. Whatever scruples he voiced disappear once his mother assumes responsibility. The speed of his obedience to her contrasts with how slowly he will come to trust God for himself. Even at Bethel his commitment will be framed as a condition: “then shall the LORD be my God” (28:21).

The string of verbs recalls, with a grim inversion, Abraham’s obedience at Moriah, where he rose, took, and went (22:3). That obedience led to an altar and to the ram God provided. This one leads to a cooking fire and a disguise. The same kind of prompt action, aimed at different ends, produces opposite results. Promptness is a virtue only when the direction is right.

“And his mother made savoury meat, such as his father loved.” The narrator again calls Isaac “his father,” not “her husband.” The marriage that began with love and comfort (24:67) has drifted far enough that a wife can cook a deceptive dish for her husband’s table. The meal that should express a family’s affection becomes a tool for dividing it.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּלֶךְ וַיִּקַּח וַיָּבֵא (vayyelekh vayyiqqakh vayyave) — and he went, and fetched, and brought
wordNotes.explanation: Three consecutive narrative verbs with no pause for reflection. Hebrew narrative often signals ready obedience this way, as when Abraham rose early, took his son, and went to the place God had told him. Here the same rhythm describes compliance with a human plan to deceive.

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah took goodly raiment of her eldest son Esau, which were with her in the house, and put them upon Jacob her younger son:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah now dresses Jacob. She takes “goodly raiment of her eldest son Esau, which were with her in the house.” These were Esau’s best garments, perhaps clothing for festive or solemn occasions kept in his mother’s care. The note that they were “with her in the house” suggests that Esau, though married and with households of his own, left his finest clothes in her keeping. Rebekah handles the possessions of one son in order to clothe the other.

Here for the first time she is said to act toward “her eldest son” and “her younger son.” The narrator makes her acknowledge the very order of birth she is working to overturn. Both sons are hers, and she will later fear losing both (v. 45), yet her action sets one against the other.

Clothing plays a recurring part in Genesis as a means of concealment and disclosure. Adam and Eve covered themselves, and God clothed them (3:7, 21). Joseph’s coat will be stripped from him, dipped in blood, and used to deceive Jacob (37:23, 31–33). Tamar will change her garments to deceive Judah (38:14), and Potiphar’s wife will produce Joseph’s garment as false evidence (39:12–18). Jacob’s disguise is the first link in a chain, and he will feel its weight when he holds his son’s bloodied coat.

Some have read Jacob in his brother’s clothing as a picture of the believer clothed in Christ. The text resists so neat a figure, because Jacob’s garments are part of a lie. The gospel offers something better than a disguise. Those who come to Christ are clothed with His righteousness openly and truthfully, as the Father’s gift (Isaiah 61:10; Galatians 3:27), and they need not pretend to be someone else in order to be received.

wordNotes.term: בִּגְדֵי ... הַחֲמֻדֹת (bigde ... hakhamudot) — goodly raiment
wordNotes.explanation: חֲמֻדֹת (khamudot) comes from the verb “to desire” and describes things precious or highly valued. Daniel is addressed as a man “greatly beloved” with the same word, and it describes the precious goods Judah gathered as spoil. Here it marks these as Esau’s choicest garments, the best he owned.

verses.bibleText: And she put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands, and upon the smooth of his neck:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she put the skins of the kids of the goats upon his hands, and upon the smooth of his neck.” Rebekah answers the exact objection Jacob raised (v. 11). The goats of that region had long, dark, coarse coats that an old man’s uncertain fingers could mistake for a hairy arm. Goats’ hair could pass for human hair in other settings as well; Michal laid a pillow of goats’ hair at the head of David’s bed to fool Saul’s messengers (1 Samuel 19:13).

The thoroughness of the disguise shows Rebekah’s determination. She has thought of the hands Isaac will grasp and the neck he will embrace. Nothing has been left to chance except the voice, which she could not alter.

In Eden God made coats of skins to clothe the guilty pair in mercy (3:21). Here skins are fitted to cover a deception. The same material serves opposite purposes depending on whose hands apply it. Proverbs describes the one who “dissembleth with his lips, and layeth up deceit within him” (26:24), and the warning that such wickedness will be exposed before the congregation fits the story that unfolds.

wordNotes.term: עֹרֹת (ʿorot) — skins
wordNotes.explanation: The plural of עוֹר (ʿor), skin or hide. It is the word used when God made “coats of skins” for Adam and Eve after the fall. In Eden skins covered shame as an act of mercy; in Isaac’s tent they cover a smooth neck to mislead a blind man.

verses.bibleText: And she gave the savoury meat and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And she gave the savoury meat and the bread, which she had prepared, into the hand of her son Jacob.” The preparations are complete. Rebekah has chosen the animals, cooked the meat, baked the bread, dressed Jacob, and covered his skin. Now she places the finished plan into his hands, and from this point he must act alone.

The handing over marks a transfer of responsibility. Jacob has been almost passive during the preparations, a figure being costumed. Once he enters his father’s presence, every word will be his own. Rebekah can prepare a meal, but she cannot speak for him; the lies he tells will belong to him. Shared schemes do not divide guilt into comfortable fractions. “The soul that sinneth, it shall die” (Ezekiel 18:20), and “every one of us shall give account of himself to God” (Romans 14:12).

wordNotes.term: לֶחֶם (lekhem) — bread
wordNotes.explanation: The common word for bread and, more broadly, food. Bread appears beside the meat as part of a complete meal. The detail recalls the bread and lentil stew for which Esau sold his birthright, so that both transactions over the inheritance are framed by food.

verses.bibleText: And he came unto his father, and said, My father: and he said, Here am I; who art thou, my son?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob goes in and speaks a single word: “My father.” Isaac answers, “Here am I; who art thou, my son?” The brevity of Jacob’s greeting betrays caution. He says no more than he must, perhaps afraid that a longer speech will give away his voice.

The exchange echoes the road to Moriah. There Isaac said to Abraham, “My father,” and Abraham answered, “Here am I, my son” (22:7). In that scene a trusting son walked beside a faithful father toward a sacrifice God Himself would provide. Now the same words frame a son approaching his father in order to deceive him. The conversation on Moriah led to the revelation of Jehovah-jireh; this one leads to a family’s fracture.

Isaac’s question shows uncertainty from the first moment. He expected Esau, but not so soon, and the voice did not fit. His unease runs through the whole scene; he questions, touches, questions again, tastes, and smells. Each test gives Jacob an opportunity to stop and confess, and each time he presses on.

“Who art thou?” is the question that will follow Jacob for twenty years. At the Jabbok a mysterious wrestler will ask, “What is thy name?” and Jacob will have to answer truthfully, “Jacob,” confessing himself the supplanter (32:27). Only after that confession will he receive a new name. Here he answers falsely; there he will answer honestly and find a blessing that cannot be stolen because it is freely given.

wordNotes.term: מִי אַתָּה בְּנִי (mi attah beni) — who art thou, my son?
wordNotes.explanation: A direct question of identity. Isaac knows a son stands before him but is unsure which one. The question returns in the chapter when Esau enters (v. 32), and in substance at the Jabbok when Jacob must give his true name. Boaz asks the same short question in the dark of the threshing floor.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob said unto his father, I am Esau thy firstborn; I have done according as thou badest me: arise, I pray thee, sit and eat of my venison, that thy soul may bless me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“I am Esau thy firstborn.” The lie is direct and complete, with no evasion or half-truth. In one phrase Jacob claims his brother’s name and his brother’s rank. He adds a second falsehood, “I have done according as thou badest me,” claiming obedience to an instruction he never received, and a third by implication, calling the meat “my venison,” as though it came from the hunt.

Jacob echoes the words Isaac had spoken to Esau: “that thy soul may bless me” (compare v. 4). He knows the script because Rebekah overheard it. Repeating Isaac’s own phrasing is meant to reassure the old man that this is the son he sent. Deception often works best when it borrows its victim’s words.

“Firstborn” is a weighty term here. Jacob had bought the birthright from Esau (25:31–34), and he might have argued that he now held the firstborn’s rights. Yet he does not say, “I am Jacob, to whom the birthright belongs.” He says, “I am Esau.” Whatever standing the earlier transaction gave him, he chose to hide behind his brother’s identity rather than make an open claim.

The ninth commandment, “Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour” (Exodus 20:16), puts in writing what conscience already knew in the patriarchs’ day. Jesus identifies lying with the character of the devil, “a liar, and the father of it” (John 8:44), while the redeemed are described as those in whose mouth “was found no guile” (Revelation 14:5). Jacob’s sin is told without softening because the God of Jacob is the God who turns deceivers into faithful witnesses.

wordNotes.term: אָנֹכִי עֵשָׂו בְּכֹרֶךָ (ʾanokhi ʿEsav bekhorekha) — I am Esau thy firstborn
wordNotes.explanation: בְּכוֹר (bekhor), firstborn, is closely related to בְּכֹרָה (bekhorah), birthright, and sounds much like בְּרָכָה (berakhah), blessing. The chapter plays on this cluster of words. Israel itself is later called God’s firstborn son, a status of privilege and responsibility that Esau despised.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac said unto his son, How is it that thou hast found it so quickly, my son? And he said, Because the LORD thy God brought it to me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac is surprised: “How is it that thou hast found it so quickly, my son?” Hunting takes time. Game must be tracked, brought down, dressed, and cooked, and the speed of this return seems implausible. Jacob answers, “Because the LORD thy God brought it to me.”

This is the gravest lie in the chapter. Jacob invokes the covenant name of God to cover a falsehood, crediting divine providence with what his mother arranged from the household flock. The third commandment forbids taking the name of the LORD in vain (Exodus 20:7), and few uses are emptier than calling God as witness to a lie. Scripture repeatedly singles out religious language used as cover for wrongdoing. Jeremiah rebukes those who steal and swear falsely and then stand in the temple saying, “We are delivered” (Jeremiah 7:9–10).

The phrase “the LORD thy God” is itself telling. Jacob does not say “my God.” At this stage the God of Abraham and Isaac is, to Jacob, his father’s God. Only at Bethel will he vow, “then shall the LORD be my God” (28:21), and only after his safe return will he build an altar named El-elohe-Israel, “God, the God of Israel” (33:20). The supplanter can use the right words about God before he knows God for himself.

The irony is sharp. God had in fact promised Jacob the blessing. Had Jacob trusted that word, he could have spoken truthfully of the LORD’s purpose without any lie at all. Instead he uses the LORD’s name to grasp what the LORD intended to give. Grace will overrule, yet the scene stands as a warning that pious vocabulary can sit alongside an unconverted heart. God’s long patience with Jacob in the years that follow measures His mercy; it does not commend Jacob’s methods.

wordNotes.term: הִקְרָה יְהוָה (hiqrah YHWH) — the LORD brought it
wordNotes.explanation: The verb קָרָה (qarah) in this causative form means to make something happen, to bring about a meeting or an outcome. Abraham’s servant used it when he prayed, “send me good speed this day,” and his prayer was answered at the well. Ruth’s “hap” to glean in Boaz’s field uses a related noun. Jacob borrows the vocabulary of providence that his grandfather’s servant used in sincere faith.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac said unto Jacob, Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac is not satisfied. “Come near, I pray thee, that I may feel thee, my son, whether thou be my very son Esau or not.” The very action Jacob dreaded (v. 12) is now on his father’s lips. The old man has heard a voice and a pious answer that do not fit the son he expects; Esau was not given to speaking about the LORD. So he turns from hearing to touch.

The request offered Jacob another chance to stop. His father’s doubt was out in the open. Yet Jacob steps forward, trusting the goatskins to do their work. Sin gathers momentum: having come this far, retreat looks more dangerous than continuing. Each lie makes confession harder, and the deceiver soon feels trapped by the demands of his own story. Proverbs observes that “a lying tongue is but for a moment” (12:19), and Hebrews warns against being “hardened through the deceitfulness of sin” (3:13).

Isaac’s reliance on touch is natural for a blind man, but it represents a choice about which evidence to trust. His ears had raised the alarm; his hands are about to overrule them.

wordNotes.term: וַאֲמֻשְׁךָ (vaʾamushekha) — that I may feel thee
wordNotes.explanation: From מוּשׁ (mush), to feel or touch, closely related to מָשַׁשׁ (mashash), to grope. It is the verb Jacob feared in verse 12. Moses warns that the disobedient will “grope at noonday, as the blind gropeth in darkness,” and Laban later “searched” all Jacob’s goods by feeling through them. Touch becomes Isaac’s test of truth, and it fails him.

verses.bibleText: And Jacob went near unto Isaac his father; and he felt him, and said, The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Jacob went near unto Isaac his father; and he felt him, and said, The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.” It is one of the most memorable sentences in Genesis. Isaac identifies the truth correctly with one sense and is misled by another. The voice tells him who is there; the hands tell him what he hopes to hear.

In Scripture the spoken word is commonly the decisive means of knowing truth. At Sinai Israel “heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice” (Deuteronomy 4:12). Faith comes by hearing (Romans 10:17), and Christ’s sheep know His voice (John 10:27). Isaac’s ears gave accurate testimony, and he set it aside in favor of what his fingers reported. There is a lesson about weighing evidence: when a clear word conflicts with appearances, the word deserves the greater trust. Isaiah describes the Messiah as one who would not judge “after the sight of his eyes” (11:3), relying instead on the discernment the Spirit gives.

The line also captures Jacob’s divided condition. He has Esau’s hands by disguise, but his voice remains his own. A costume can change what is felt, yet it cannot change who a person is. The rest of Jacob’s story shows God working on the inner man until voice and hands belong to the same honest person.

Isaac senses the contradiction and lacks the resolve to settle it by direct challenge. His wish to bless Esau may have made him eager to dismiss the discordant evidence.

wordNotes.term: הַקֹּל קוֹל יַעֲקֹב (haqqol qol Yaʿaqov) — the voice is Jacob’s voice
wordNotes.explanation: קוֹל (qol) means voice or sound. Isaac’s ear correctly identifies the speaker even when his hands are fooled. Scripture often treats the heard voice as the surest witness, whether God’s voice at Sinai or the Shepherd’s voice recognized by His sheep.

verses.bibleText: And he discerned him not, because his hands were hairy, as his brother Esau's hands: so he blessed him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he discerned him not, because his hands were hairy, as his brother Esau’s hands: so he blessed him.” The narrator explains the success of the deception in a single clause: the disguise worked, and Isaac failed to recognize his son.

“So he blessed him” raises a question, since the formal blessing comes only in verses 27–29, after further questions and the meal. The verb can describe a greeting or the beginning of a process, and the narrator may be stating the outcome before telling how it unfolded. Either way, the decisive turn has come. The hairy hands have broken Isaac’s resistance, and from here he moves toward the blessing.

The Hebrew verb for “discerned” becomes a thread through the Jacob and Joseph stories. Jacob’s sons will bring Joseph’s coat and say, “know now whether it be thy son’s coat or no,” and Jacob “knew it” (37:32–33). Tamar will say to Judah, “Discern, I pray thee,” and Judah will “acknowledge” his pledge (38:25–26). Joseph will recognize his brothers while they fail to recognize him (42:7–8). Failures of recognition, many of them engineered by deceit, run through the family until God brings the truth to light. What begins in Isaac’s tent reaches across a generation.

The verse also marks the limits of human perception. Isaac could not see, and his other senses misled him. God is never misled: “all things are naked and opened unto the eyes of him with whom we have to do” (Hebrews 4:13). The blessing proceeds because He permits it, and His purpose for Jacob stands in the midst of the fraud.

wordNotes.term: וְלֹא הִכִּירוֹ (velo hikkiro) — and he discerned him not
wordNotes.explanation: The verb נָכַר (nakar) in this form means to recognize or identify. It recurs at key moments in the family history: Jacob recognizing Joseph’s bloodied coat, Judah acknowledging his pledge before Tamar, and Joseph recognizing brothers who did not recognize him. The repetition ties Jacob’s deception of his father to the deceptions later practiced on him.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Art thou my very son Esau? And he said, I am.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Art thou my very son Esau? And he said, I am.” Isaac asks one last time, now as directly as he can. It is the plainest question in the chapter, and Jacob gives the plainest lie, a single Hebrew word meaning “I.” Perhaps he answers so briefly to give his voice as little exposure as possible.

Each missed opportunity to turn back makes the next lie easier. Jacob has already lied about his identity (v. 19) and about the source of the meat (v. 20); now he repeats the claim to his father’s face in answer to a direct question. Repeated deception hardens the heart, and what began with hesitation has become bold.

Readers who know the rest of Scripture may hear a contrast in this short reply. God names Himself “I AM” (Exodus 3:14), and Jesus declared, “Before Abraham was, I am” (John 8:58). Jacob’s “I am” claims to be someone he is not; God’s self-disclosure is the speech of the One who is exactly what He says. “God is not a man, that he should lie” (Numbers 23:19), and those who belong to Him are called to put away lying and speak truth to their neighbors (Ephesians 4:25).

wordNotes.term: אָנִי (ʾani) — I am
wordNotes.explanation: Hebrew can answer a question of identity with the pronoun alone: “I.” Jacob’s one-word reply is the barest possible affirmation. The same pronoun stands in God’s declarations, “I am he,” in Isaiah, and the Greek “I am” of Jesus’ sayings carries that divine self-identification.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Bring it near to me, and I will eat of my son's venison, that my soul may bless thee. And he brought it near to him, and he did eat: and he brought him wine, and he drank.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac now calls for the meal: “Bring it near to me, and I will eat of my son’s venison, that my soul may bless thee.” The meal is the setting he had planned for the blessing. The narrator reports simply that Jacob brought it, Isaac ate, and Jacob brought wine and he drank. Nothing suggests that the taste aroused suspicion; Rebekah’s cooking did its work.

Isaac’s taste fails him as his touch did. Goat from the flock, well seasoned, passes for wild game. The appetite that first drew Isaac’s affection toward Esau (25:28) now betrays him. What a person craves can become the means of his undoing when appetite governs judgment. Esau sold his birthright for a meal; Isaac misdirects his blessing over one. Proverbs counsels the guest at a ruler’s table to “put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite” (23:2), since dainties can be deceitful food.

The wine completes the picture of a festive meal. The word here is the ordinary term for fermented wine. Scripture reports its use in patriarchal times without commending it, and it repeatedly warns that wine clouds judgment: “Wine is a mocker” (Proverbs 20:1), and rulers are told that it is not for them to drink, “lest they drink, and forget the law” (Proverbs 31:4–5). A blind old man eating and drinking is in no condition to see through a ruse, and weighty decisions call for a clear mind.

wordNotes.term: יַיִן (yayin) — wine
wordNotes.explanation: The common Hebrew word for fermented wine, used of Noah’s drunkenness and of the drink Proverbs calls a mocker. It differs from תִּירוֹשׁ (tirosh) in the blessing of verse 28, which names the fresh produce of the vineyard. The narrative mentions Isaac’s drinking without comment, but the setting underscores how impaired his judgment was.

verses.bibleText: And his father Isaac said unto him, Come near now, and kiss me, my son.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Come near now, and kiss me, my son.” Isaac’s request is affectionate and likely part of the customary approach to a blessing, a gesture of closeness before solemn words. It may also be one more test, since an embrace will bring him near enough to smell his son.

The kiss is among the saddest details in the scene. A sign of love becomes the final act of deceit. Scripture records other kisses turned to betrayal: Joab took Amasa by the beard to kiss him and struck him with the sword (2 Samuel 20:9–10), Absalom kissed the people to steal their hearts (2 Samuel 15:5–6), and Judas betrayed the Son of man with a kiss (Luke 22:48). Proverbs observes that “the kisses of an enemy are deceitful” (27:6). Jacob is not his father’s enemy, yet the kiss he gives carries the same falseness.

Kisses return in Jacob’s story with healing meaning. When he meets Rachel at the well he kisses her and weeps (29:11). When he finally faces Esau after twenty years, Esau runs to meet him, falls on his neck, and kisses him, and the two brothers weep together (33:4). The deceitful kiss given to the father will be answered by the brother’s kiss of reconciliation, a grace Jacob had not earned.

wordNotes.term: וּשְׁקָה־לִּי (ushqah-li) — and kiss me
wordNotes.explanation: From נָשַׁק (nashaq), to kiss, used for family affection, greeting, and reconciliation. The same verb describes Jacob kissing Rachel at the well and Joab’s treacherous kiss of Amasa. Context, not the gesture itself, determines whether a kiss expresses love or masks betrayal.

verses.bibleText: And he came near, and kissed him: and he smelled the smell of his raiment, and blessed him, and said, See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Jacob comes near and kisses his father. Isaac catches “the smell of his raiment,” Esau’s garments, steeped in the scent of open country, and his last doubt dissolves. Then the blessing begins, and the narrative shifts into the elevated, parallel lines of Hebrew poetry: “See, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field which the LORD hath blessed.”

The fragrance shapes the imagery. Isaac thinks of a field rich with growth, alive with herbs and blossom, the kind of land Canaan could be in its fruitful season. A field “which the LORD hath blessed” points toward the land God promised to Abraham’s seed (12:7; 13:15; 26:3). Isaac believes he is blessing the hunter, yet his words turn the field from a hunting ground into a cultivated inheritance. Without knowing it, he describes the portion God had appointed for Jacob.

Here the patriarch speaks with prophetic authority. The blessing is no incantation that works apart from God; it is a declaration God honors because it agrees with His own purpose. Hebrews remembers it as an act of faith: “By faith Isaac blessed Jacob and Esau concerning things to come” (11:20). The fraud surrounding the words does not empty them, because God had chosen Jacob long before. The trick contributed nothing to that purpose and could not defeat it. The LORD took a sinful scheme and steered it toward an end He had already set, and the blessing rested on His choice rather than on Jacob’s cleverness.

Fragrance in Scripture often accompanies acceptance before God. Noah’s offering rose as “a sweet savour” (8:21), and Christ’s self-giving is “a sweetsmelling savour” to God (Ephesians 5:2). Jacob’s borrowed scent is a counterfeit, yet the gospel holds out the reality. Believers are accepted because they are joined to Christ by faith, so that they become “unto God a sweet savour of Christ” (2 Corinthians 2:15). That acceptance requires no false identity; it is the Father’s open gift.

Isaac names the LORD as the source of the field’s fruitfulness. Whatever his failures, he still knows from whose hand abundance comes.

wordNotes.term: רֵיחַ (reakh) — smell
wordNotes.explanation: The noun for scent or aroma, used of the “sweet savour” of Noah’s sacrifice and frequently of offerings acceptable to God. Here it is the smell of Esau’s clothes that convinces Isaac. Paul draws on the same imagery when he speaks of believers as the fragrance of Christ, using the Greek equivalent found in the Septuagint.

wordNotes.term: שָׂדֶה אֲשֶׁר בֵּרֲכוֹ יְהוָה (sadeh asher berakho YHWH) — a field which the LORD hath blessed
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase pictures fertile land under God’s favor. It anticipates Moses’ blessing on Joseph’s territory, “blessed of the LORD be his land,” and recalls Isaac’s own hundredfold harvest when “the LORD blessed him.” Fruitfulness is credited to God, not to the farmer or the hunter.

verses.bibleText: Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Therefore God give thee of the dew of heaven, and the fatness of the earth, and plenty of corn and wine.” The blessing moves from sky to soil. Dew comes first. In a land with a long rainless summer, the dew settling on the hills night after night carried crops through the dry months. Moses would bless Joseph’s land “for the dew” (Deuteronomy 33:13), and the withholding of dew was a mark of judgment, as in Elijah’s day (1 Kings 17:1) and after the return from exile (Haggai 1:10). Dew is a gift from above, entirely beyond human control.

“The fatness of the earth” describes rich, productive ground. Corn and wine, grain and new wine, are the staples of a prosperous agricultural life, often paired with oil in the covenant promises to Israel in the land (Deuteronomy 7:13; 11:14). Isaac’s words anticipate the life Israel would enjoy in Canaan when walking with God.

The word translated “wine” here is tirosh, the fresh yield of the vineyard at harvest, the juice as it comes from the grape. It is a term of agricultural plenty, regularly paired with grain, and distinct from the ordinary word for the drink in Isaac’s cup in verse 25. The blessing celebrates the bounty of the land God gives.

The heart of the line is “God give thee.” Isaac uses the general name Elohim, the Creator who rules over nature. Material and spiritual blessing are not set in opposition here. Within the covenant, land and harvest were tokens of God’s faithfulness, and enjoying them was meant to lead to thanksgiving and obedience: “When thou hast eaten and art full, then thou shalt bless the LORD thy God” (Deuteronomy 8:10). The New Testament carries the principle forward. Every good gift comes from above (James 1:17), and those who seek first God’s kingdom find that their Father knows what they need (Matthew 6:32–33).

wordNotes.term: טַל הַשָּׁמַיִם (tal hashshamayim) — the dew of heaven
wordNotes.explanation: טַל (tal) is the night moisture that waters vegetation in the dry season. It appears in blessings as a sign of God’s gentle, life-giving care: God promises to be “as the dew unto Israel,” and the restored remnant is promised that “the heavens shall give their dew.”

wordNotes.term: דָּגָן וְתִירֹשׁ (dagan vetirosh) — corn and wine
wordNotes.explanation: דָּגָן (dagan) is grain, and תִּירוֹשׁ (tirosh) the fresh produce of the vineyard, the new wine of harvest. The pair, often joined with oil, sums up the fruitfulness of the land in covenant blessings. Hosea reminds Israel that it was God who gave the corn, the wine, and the oil.

verses.bibleText: Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother's sons bow down to thee: cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be he that blesseth thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The blessing moves from land to nations. “Let people serve thee, and nations bow down to thee: be lord over thy brethren, and let thy mother’s sons bow down to thee: cursed be every one that curseth thee, and blessed be he that blesseth thee.” Three movements stand out: dominion over peoples, preeminence within the family, and the protective promise first given to Abraham.

“Be lord over thy brethren” is exactly what the oracle had foretold: “the elder shall serve the younger” (25:23). Isaac, intending to place Esau over Jacob, confirms the reverse. His attempt to override God’s word becomes the very means of fulfilling it. “Thy mother’s sons” is a poetic parallel for brothers and kin, embracing Esau and the nation that would descend from him (36:1–43). The fulfillment unfolds in Israel’s history, most clearly when David placed garrisons throughout Edom and “all they of Edom became David’s servants” (2 Samuel 8:14).

The closing line echoes God’s word to Abraham: “I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee” (12:3). In speaking it, Isaac hands on the core of the Abrahamic covenant, and the line of promise now runs through Jacob. Balaam, hired to curse Israel, would find himself unable to reverse what God had blessed and would repeat the same words: “Blessed is he that blesseth thee, and cursed is he that curseth thee” (Numbers 24:9).

The vision of nations bowing reaches beyond Israel’s political fortunes. God intended the nations to see His wisdom in Israel and to seek the LORD (Deuteronomy 4:6; Zechariah 8:22–23). That purpose finds its goal in Jacob’s greatest descendant, the King of whom it was sung, “all nations shall serve him” (Psalm 72:11), and to whom all authority in heaven and earth has been given (Matthew 28:18). Through Christ the blessing of Abraham comes to the Gentiles (Galatians 3:14), and the nations come and worship before the Lamb (Revelation 15:4) rather than before an earthly empire.

That a blessing so rich in promise was obtained by a lie remains painful. Yet God’s purpose is not held hostage by human sin. He works through flawed people without approving their flaws, and He carries His promise forward until it reaches its fulfillment in Christ.

wordNotes.term: גְבִיר (gevir) — lord
wordNotes.explanation: A rare word meaning master or ruler, found in the Old Testament only here and in Isaac’s words to Esau in verse 37. It belongs to the same family as גְּבִירָה (gevirah), the title of a queen mother, and expresses real authority. It confirms the prenatal oracle that the elder would serve the younger.

wordNotes.term: אֹרְרֶיךָ אָרוּר (ʾorerekha ʾarur) — cursed be every one that curseth thee
wordNotes.explanation: The wording closely reflects God’s promise to Abraham and reappears in Balaam’s oracle over Israel. It declares that God will treat the friends and foes of the chosen line as His own friends and foes, a protection now attached to Jacob.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, as soon as Isaac had made an end of blessing Jacob, and Jacob was yet scarce gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, that Esau his brother came in from his hunting.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, as soon as Isaac had made an end of blessing Jacob, and Jacob was yet scarce gone out from the presence of Isaac his father, that Esau his brother came in from his hunting.” The timing is razor thin. The Hebrew uses an emphatic construction, “he had only just gone out,” to stress how narrowly the brothers missed each other.

Had Esau arrived a few minutes earlier, the scheme would have collapsed, and given the fury he later reveals (v. 41), violence might have broken out in the tent. The narrator’s attention to timing invites the reader to see Providence at work even within a story of human plotting. God did not devise the deception, yet He governed the hour so that His purpose for Jacob stood and a deadly confrontation was averted. The servant at the well had seen Rebekah appear “before he had done speaking” (24:15); here, too, the moment is ordered.

Esau “came in from his hunting,” returning with honest success. He had done what his father asked, and in this sense he is the wronged party; the narrator lets the reader feel his loss. Yet Esau’s earlier contempt for the birthright (25:34) and his marriages outside the covenant (26:34–35) show that he now seeks a privilege he had already treated lightly. Both truths stand together in the story.

wordNotes.term: אַךְ יָצֹא יָצָא (ʾakh yatso yatsa) — was yet scarce gone out
wordNotes.explanation: The adverb אַךְ (ʾakh), “only, just,” combined with the doubled verb “going out he went out,” emphasizes that Jacob had barely left. Hebrew uses such doubling to intensify. The construction highlights the precise timing that kept the brothers apart, much as Rebekah arrived at the well before the servant finished praying.

verses.bibleText: And he also had made savoury meat, and brought it unto his father, and said unto his father, Let my father arise, and eat of his son's venison, that thy soul may bless me.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he also had made savoury meat, and brought it unto his father.” Esau has done everything Isaac asked: hunted, cooked, and served. He enters with confident formality: “Let my father arise, and eat of his son’s venison, that thy soul may bless me.” He speaks of his father in the third person, a respectful form of address, and expects a warm welcome.

The contrast with Jacob is sharp. Jacob came in with one timid word (v. 18); Esau comes in with a full sentence, sure of his place. His confidence is natural, for he has no idea what has happened. The reader, knowing what Esau does not, feels the blow before it falls.

“He also” is a poignant phrase. Esau has prepared a meal just as Jacob did, but too late. His tragedy is not a lack of effort. He sought the blessing as a reward for a meal, on the same terms by which he had lost the birthright, as if holy things could be traded for food. God’s gifts cannot be earned by service, and those who once despised them cannot reclaim them on demand (Hebrews 12:16–17). Jesus’ parable of the virgins pictures the same painful lateness: those who arrive after the door is shut call, “Lord, Lord, open to us” (Matthew 25:10–11).

wordNotes.term: יָקֻם אָבִי (yaqum ʾavi) — let my father arise
wordNotes.explanation: A third-person form of request, more deferential than Jacob’s direct “arise, I pray thee” in verse 19. Speaking of the listener in the third person was a courteous way to address a superior, as Judah does before Joseph. Esau’s respect for his father is real, even though his request comes too late.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac his father said unto him, Who art thou? And he said, I am thy son, thy firstborn Esau.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Isaac his father said unto him, Who art thou?” It is the same question he put to Jacob (v. 18), but this time without “my son.” Esau answers, “I am thy son, thy firstborn Esau.” He leads with the relationship and only then gives his name, whereas Jacob had led with Esau’s name to make the claim stick.

The answer brings the truth crashing in. Isaac has already blessed someone who claimed to be Esau, and now the real Esau stands before him. His question expresses more than confusion; it is the first shock of recognition. He realizes that his ears were right and that he overrode them.

Esau calls himself “thy firstborn,” which is true by birth and painful in the light of what he had done. The firstborn’s birthright he had sold under oath (25:33), and now he claims the title as though the sale had meant nothing. Esau represents those who want the privileges of a spiritual heritage while treating its responsibilities with indifference. Hebrews calls him “profane” (12:16), a man who treated holy things as common. The title of firstborn without the faith that should accompany it could not secure the blessing.

The scene is tragic as well as instructive. Esau is not drawn as a mere villain. He is a son who loved his father and did what he was asked, and the narrative refuses easy categories.

wordNotes.term: בִּנְךָ בְכֹרְךָ עֵשָׂו (binkha vekhorekha ʿEsav) — thy son, thy firstborn Esau
wordNotes.explanation: Esau orders his self-description by relationship: son, then firstborn, then name. Jacob had said, “I am Esau thy firstborn.” The difference is subtle, yet it shows each brother’s concern: Esau stresses his bond with his father, while Jacob had stressed the identity he was borrowing. The firstborn status Esau names is the one he earlier sold.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac trembled very exceedingly, and said, Who? where is he that hath taken venison, and brought it me, and I have eaten of all before thou camest, and have blessed him? yea, and he shall be blessed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Isaac trembled very exceedingly.” The Hebrew stacks its intensifiers: he trembled a great trembling, to the utmost. The old man is shaken to the core. He asks, “Who? where is he that hath taken venison, and brought it me, and I have eaten of all before thou camest, and have blessed him?” Then he adds, “yea, and he shall be blessed.”

Isaac’s trembling is more than the shock of being tricked. He sees that he has been overruled. He had set out to give the blessing to Esau against God’s declared will, and in the very act his words went to Jacob. Balaam would later learn that he could speak only what God put in his mouth (Numbers 22:38; 23:20); Isaac now discovers the same thing about himself. A blessing aimed against the divine purpose had been redirected by a stronger hand. His trembling is the fear of a man who suddenly realizes he has been resisting God.

“Yea, and he shall be blessed.” Here Isaac’s faith comes back to the surface. He does not curse Jacob, retract his words, or try to reassign the blessing. He accepts that what was spoken stands. This is why Hebrews counts him among the faithful (11:20). The blessing holds because God had chosen Jacob, and Isaac now acknowledges it; his words have no power apart from that choice. From this point he stops resisting. When Jacob departs, Isaac will bless him again knowingly and give him “the blessing of Abraham” (28:3–4).

Isaac also had to face his own share in the matter. His favoritism, his secret plan, and his disregard of the oracle created the opening that his wife and son exploited. He could hardly curse Jacob for a deception his own disobedience had invited. Recognizing God’s hand, he submits.

The verse carries both comfort and warning. God’s purposes cannot be defeated by human plans, including the plans of His own people: “the counsel of the LORD, that shall stand” (Proverbs 19:21; Isaiah 46:10). Yet those who resist His revealed will may discover too late that they have been working against Him.

wordNotes.term: וַיֶּחֱרַד ... חֲרָדָה גְּדֹלָה עַד־מְאֹד (vayyekherad ... kharadah gedolah ʿad-meʾod) — trembled very exceedingly
wordNotes.explanation: The verb חָרַד (kharad), to tremble, is joined to its own noun and two intensifiers: literally “he trembled a great trembling, exceedingly.” The same verb describes the whole people trembling at Sinai and Saul’s heart trembling before the Philistine host. It conveys violent inner shock, not mild surprise.

wordNotes.term: גַּם־בָּרוּךְ יִהְיֶה (gam-barukh yihyeh) — yea, and he shall be blessed
wordNotes.explanation: The particle גַּם (gam), “also, indeed,” adds emphasis: the blessing stands. Isaac affirms that what he spoke cannot be undone. Balaam would later confess the same principle, “he hath blessed; and I cannot reverse it,” because God stands behind the word.

verses.bibleText: And when Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry, and said unto his father, Bless me, even me also, O my father.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And when Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with a great and exceeding bitter cry, and said unto his father, Bless me, even me also, O my father.” The cry is loud and raw, a wail of loss. Almost the same phrase describes Mordecai’s lament when he learned of the decree to destroy his people (Esther 4:1). Esau grasps at once that something has happened that cannot be undone.

His plea, “Bless me, even me also,” is broken speech. He does not ask Isaac to reverse the blessing given to Jacob; he seems to know that is impossible. He asks for something of his own. It is the cry of a son who wants his father’s favor and finds that it has already been given away.

Readers should not harden themselves against Esau’s anguish. He had been wronged by his brother’s deceit, and his grief is real. Yet the narrative also shows that his sorrow concerned the loss, not the attitude that had made the loss possible. Hebrews draws the lesson: when Esau later wanted to inherit the blessing, “he was rejected: for he found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears” (12:17). His tears sought a change of outcome, not a change of heart. He wanted the blessing back without renouncing the profane spirit that had sold the birthright.

Scripture distinguishes the sorrow of the world, which mourns consequences, from godly sorrow, which works repentance (2 Corinthians 7:10). Esau’s cry belongs to the first kind. It is possible to weep bitterly over lost privileges and still not turn to God. The prodigal, by contrast, came to himself and went home to say, “Father, I have sinned” (Luke 15:18). Esau’s cry stands as a warning to every generation: the time to value God’s gifts is while they are offered. “Seek ye the LORD while he may be found” (Isaiah 55:6).

wordNotes.term: צְעָקָה גְּדֹלָה וּמָרָה (tseʿaqah gedolah umarah) — a great and exceeding bitter cry
wordNotes.explanation: צְעָקָה (tseʿaqah) is an outcry of distress, here intensified as “great and bitter.” Mordecai’s lament in Susa uses nearly identical words, and Egypt’s “great cry” on the night of the firstborn uses the same noun. The phrase marks Esau’s grief as the anguish of irreversible loss.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac’s reply is brief and crushing: “Thy brother came with subtilty, and hath taken away thy blessing.” He names the one responsible and calls the act what it was. The word rendered “subtilty” is the ordinary Hebrew term for deceit or fraud. Isaac upholds the blessing, yet he does not excuse the way it was obtained.

That combination matters. Isaac acknowledges both that Jacob deceived and that the blessing stands. Scripture never treats Jacob’s trick as admirable. The same word family returns when Laban substitutes Leah for Rachel and Jacob protests, “wherefore then hast thou beguiled me?” (29:25). Jacob’s sons will answer Shechem and Hamor “deceitfully” (34:13). The deceiver will be deceived, and deceit will pass to the next generation. When Jesus later greets Nathanael as “an Israelite indeed, in whom is no guile” (John 1:47), the words read like a quiet reversal of the old Jacob.

“Hath taken away thy blessing” reflects Esau’s expectation and Isaac’s original intention. In God’s design the blessing had never been Esau’s to lose. Before the twins were born, “that the purpose of God according to election might stand,” it was said that the elder would serve the younger (Romans 9:11–12). Jacob seized by stealth what God would have given by grace. The tragedy is not that Jacob received the blessing, but that he received it in a way that cost him twenty years of exile and sorrow. Proverbs puts it plainly: “Bread of deceit is sweet to a man; but afterwards his mouth shall be filled with gravel” (20:17).

wordNotes.term: בְּמִרְמָה (bemirmah) — with subtilty
wordNotes.explanation: מִרְמָה (mirmah) means deceit, fraud, or treachery. Its verb appears when Jacob accuses Laban of having “beguiled” him, and the noun when Jacob’s sons speak “deceitfully” to Shechem. Jesus’ description of Nathanael as without “guile” uses the Greek word that commonly renders this term in the Septuagint.

verses.bibleText: And he said, Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing. And he said, Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Esau bursts out: “Is not he rightly named Jacob? for he hath supplanted me these two times: he took away my birthright; and, behold, now he hath taken away my blessing.” The name Jacob was linked to his birth, when he came out grasping Esau’s heel (25:26). Esau now reads it as describing a heel-catcher, one who trips up another from behind.

The verb Esau uses, “supplanted,” comes from the same stem as the name. The prophets later use it of treachery within families: “every brother will utterly supplant” (Jeremiah 9:4). Hosea recalls that Jacob “took his brother by the heel in the womb, and by his strength he had power with God” (Hosea 12:3). Esau’s reading of the name is not wrong; it describes the character Jacob has displayed. Only God would later give him a new name to match a changed heart (32:28).

Esau’s complaint mixes truth with self-justification. Of the two occasions he names, only one involved deception. The birthright he sold freely, under oath, for bread and lentil stew (25:33–34). He now recasts that transaction as theft and takes no responsibility for it. He sees, too late, the value of what he despised, and he rewrites his history to make himself solely the victim. The pattern is as old as Eden, where blame was passed rather than sin confessed (3:12–13).

Notice the wordplay on his lips: birthright (bekorah) and blessing (berakhah) sound almost alike. To Esau they were separate prizes; Scripture treats them as belonging together. The one who scorned the first could not secure the second (Hebrews 12:16–17).

Then Esau asks, “Hast thou not reserved a blessing for me?” He hopes some portion has been held back.

wordNotes.term: וַיַּעְקְבֵנִי (vayyaʿqeveni) — he hath supplanted me
wordNotes.explanation: The verb עָקַב (ʿaqav) is related to עָקֵב (ʿaqev), heel, and to the name יַעֲקֹב (Yaʿaqov). It means to overreach or trip up from behind. Jeremiah uses it of brothers who deceive one another, and Hosea recalls Jacob’s grasp of the heel as the beginning of his story.

wordNotes.term: בְּכֹרָתִי ... בִּרְכָתִי (bekhorati ... birkhati) — my birthright ... my blessing
wordNotes.explanation: The two nouns differ mainly by the order of their consonants, a deliberate play on sound. The birthright concerned headship and inheritance; the blessing conveyed the prophetic word of favor. Hebrews joins Esau’s sale of the one with his rejection when he sought the other.
