verses.bibleText: And Isaac answered and said unto Esau, Behold, I have made him thy lord, and all his brethren have I given to him for servants; and with corn and wine have I sustained him: and what shall I do now unto thee, my son?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac lays out what has been given: “Behold, I have made him thy lord, and all his brethren have I given to him for servants; and with corn and wine have I sustained him: and what shall I do now unto thee, my son?” He summarizes the blessing of verses 28–29, rule over kin and the provision of grain and wine. All of it now belongs to Jacob.

Isaac speaks as the one who has “made” and “given,” the language of a patriarch whose words carry authority. Yet he knows that the authority behind them is God’s. What has been spoken under God’s witness cannot be divided or handed over to another. His question, “what shall I do now unto thee?” is the helpless cry of a father who meant to give his favorite everything and now has nothing of that kind left.

The irony is complete. Isaac had intended to make Esau lord over Jacob. Instead Jacob has been made lord over Esau, exactly as the oracle declared (25:23). Isaac’s private plan has produced the very outcome he wished to prevent. “There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD” (Proverbs 21:30).

Isaac still calls Esau “my son.” His affection survives the loss, and that tenderness anticipates God’s own patience toward Edom. Even in the law Israel was told, “Thou shalt not abhor an Edomite; for he is thy brother” (Deuteronomy 23:7).

wordNotes.term: סְמַכְתִּיו (semakhtiv) — I have sustained him
wordNotes.explanation: The verb סָמַךְ (samakh) means to lean upon, support, or uphold. The psalmist uses it when he says, “the LORD sustained me,” and David prays, “uphold me with thy free spirit.” Isaac describes the grain and wine of the blessing as provision that will hold Jacob up.

verses.bibleText: And Esau said unto his father, Hast thou but one blessing, my father? bless me, even me also, O my father. And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Esau presses again: “Hast thou but one blessing, my father? bless me, even me also, O my father. And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.” It is one of the most poignant lines in Genesis. The strong hunter weeps aloud before his father.

The question deserves a careful answer. God’s goodness is not scarce; “The LORD is good to all” (Psalm 145:9), and He is “rich unto all that call upon him” (Romans 10:12). Yet the particular blessing at stake, the covenant headship, the land, and the line through which the promised Seed would come, could rest on only one heir, and it had been assigned to Jacob before birth. Esau wanted that unique inheritance while remaining indifferent to the God who gave it and the life it required. Had he sought the LORD with a changed heart, he could still have known the mercy of the God of Abraham, as many outside the chosen line did through faith. God’s dealings with nations and persons answer to their response (Jeremiah 18:7–10).

“And Esau lifted up his voice, and wept.” Hebrews comments that he “found no place of repentance, though he sought it carefully with tears” (12:17). The repentance he could not find is most naturally the reversal of the decision: Isaac could not take back what had been spoken. Esau’s tears aimed to change the outcome, not himself. They were tears over a lost advantage, not over sin. That is why Esau stands in the New Testament as a warning, a man who traded a lasting inheritance for a passing appetite and could not later buy it back.

His resentment at Jacob’s favor resembles the elder brother in Jesus’ parable, who would not rejoice when the father welcomed the prodigal (Luke 15:28–30). Both were unwilling to celebrate grace shown to another.

Yet the story does not end with Esau’s tears. He would become a nation, receive a word from his father, and many years later meet Jacob with an embrace (33:4). God’s verdict on Esau’s choices did not cancel His care for Esau’s descendants; He later gave them Mount Seir and forbade Israel to take it (Deuteronomy 2:5).

wordNotes.term: הַבְרָכָה אַחַת הִוא־לְךָ (haverakhah akhat hiv-lekha) — hast thou but one blessing?
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “Is it one blessing you have?” The question assumes that the father’s store of blessing might hold more. Isaac’s answer shows that the covenant blessing was singular and already given. Hebrews uses Esau’s rejection as a warning, while Jeremiah shows that God’s announced dealings respond to whether people turn from evil.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּבְךְּ (vayyevk) — and wept
wordNotes.explanation: From בָּכָה (bakhah), to weep aloud. Weeping marks many turning points in Jacob’s family: Jacob weeps when he meets Rachel, and the brothers weep together when Esau embraces Jacob years later. Here the tears are bitter, but they are not the last tears between these brothers.

verses.bibleText: And Isaac his father answered and said unto him, Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Isaac finally answers Esau’s plea: “Behold, thy dwelling shall be the fatness of the earth, and of the dew of heaven from above.” The narrator does not call this a blessing. Verse 27 said that Isaac “blessed him and said”; here Isaac simply “answered and said.” And the name of God, present in Jacob’s blessing (v. 28), is missing.

The King James rendering “of” suggests that Esau shares in the same gifts as Jacob, rich soil and dew. That reading is grammatically possible. The Hebrew preposition min, however, can also mean “away from,” and that sense suits the setting better. Isaac has just said he has nothing left to give (v. 37); he would hardly turn around and repeat Jacob’s portion. Read in that sense, Esau’s home would lie far from the earth’s fatness and far from heaven’s dew, and the words describe the land Esau’s descendants would occupy south and east of the Dead Sea, a region of rugged red sandstone heights and dry country, far less fertile than the hills of Canaan. Isaac takes the very terms he used for Jacob and turns them inside out.

Even the order of the words is reversed. Jacob’s blessing began with heaven and moved to earth; Esau’s word begins with earth and ends with heaven. The reversed sequence underlines the reversed lot. Jacob’s portion hangs on God’s gift from above; Esau’s existence will be marked by distance from that abundance.

This does not mean Edom would be left without provision. Esau’s line produced kings before Israel had any (36:31), and God later gave Mount Seir to Esau as a possession and forbade Israel to seize it (Deuteronomy 2:5). Yet the covenant inheritance, the land of promise and the line of the Messiah, belonged to Jacob. Isaac’s word to Esau is something less than a blessing and something short of a full curse: a sober forecast of life lived apart from the covenant’s richest gifts.

wordNotes.term: מִשְׁמַנֵּי הָאָרֶץ (mishmanne haʾarets) — of the fatness of the earth
wordNotes.explanation: The prefix מִ (mi-, from min) can mark a portion (“of, some of”) or separation (“away from”). In verse 28 it gave Jacob a share in the earth’s richness; here the same form, with “fatness” and “dew” in reversed order, most naturally means distance from that richness. Malachi later describes Esau’s heritage as laid waste, consistent with a harsher lot.

verses.bibleText: And by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother; and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And by thy sword shalt thou live, and shalt serve thy brother; and it shall come to pass when thou shalt have the dominion, that thou shalt break his yoke from off thy neck.” The hunter’s way of life becomes the nation’s. Edom’s people would live by force, holding the trade routes that crossed their rugged territory and raiding their neighbors.

“Shalt serve thy brother” repeats the oracle spoken before birth (25:23), and Israel’s history bears it out in detail. Saul fought against Edom (1 Samuel 14:47), and David subdued it and placed garrisons throughout the land (2 Samuel 8:14). Edom stirred against Solomon (1 Kings 11:14–22) and broke free under Jehoram (2 Kings 8:20–22). Amaziah won back part of it (2 Kings 14:7), Uzziah restored Elath (2 Kings 14:22), and in the days of Ahaz Edom threw off Judah’s control (2 Kings 16:6; 2 Chronicles 28:17). Centuries later the Idumeans, as they were then called, were conquered and absorbed into the Jewish state, and in time an Idumean family, the Herods, ruled Judea under Rome.

“When thou shalt have the dominion” renders a rare verb that seems to mean to roam at large or grow restless. Esau’s descendants would not settle into subjection; they would chafe against it until they broke the yoke. Isaac’s word therefore holds both servitude and release, a mixed and unsettled lot.

The long fulfillment of these words confirms that Isaac spoke by faith “concerning things to come” (Hebrews 11:20). The accuracy of the forecast about Esau gives confidence that the blessing on Jacob would be fulfilled as well. The God who “removeth kings, and setteth up kings” (Daniel 2:21) and fixes the bounds of the nations (Acts 17:26) carried both lines of history forward according to His word.

Esau’s portion also carries a warning. To live by the sword is to rely on one’s own strength. Jesus said that “all they that take the sword shall perish with the sword” (Matthew 26:52), and the psalmist set the covenant people’s confidence elsewhere: “Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the LORD our God” (Psalm 20:7).

wordNotes.term: עַל־חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה (ʿal-kharbekha tikhyeh) — by thy sword shalt thou live
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “upon your sword you will live,” meaning that the sword will be the means of livelihood. The phrase forecasts Edom’s warlike character, condemned by Obadiah for violence against his brother Jacob. Jesus’ warning about those who take the sword shows where such dependence leads.

wordNotes.term: תָּרִיד (tarid) — thou shalt have the dominion
wordNotes.explanation: From the rare verb רוּד (rud), which appears to mean to roam freely or be restless. In Jeremiah Israel boasts, “We are lords; we will come no more unto thee,” using the same verb for throwing off restraint. Here it describes Edom’s restless striving until it shakes off Jacob’s yoke.

verses.bibleText: And Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing wherewith his father blessed him: and Esau said in his heart, The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then will I slay my brother Jacob.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing wherewith his father blessed him.” Grief hardens into hatred. The Hebrew verb describes a grudge held and nursed, hostility that lies in wait. It is the word Joseph’s brothers use when they fear he will “hate” them once their father is dead (50:15), and it describes the archers who “hated” Joseph (49:23).

Esau speaks “in his heart,” to himself: “The days of mourning for my father are at hand; then will I slay my brother Jacob.” He resolves on murder but postpones it out of regard for his father. Like Isaac (v. 2), he assumes the old man will die soon, and he plans to wait until the mourning is over. In fact Isaac would live for decades, and the two brothers would bury him together (35:29).

The resolve to kill a brother puts Esau on Cain’s road. Cain nursed his anger until it became murder (4:5–8), and John holds him up as the example of hatred that springs from the evil one: “Not as Cain, who was of that wicked one, and slew his brother” (1 John 3:12). Jesus taught that anger in the heart already shares the guilt of murder (Matthew 5:21–22), and John states it plainly: “Whosoever hateth his brother is a murderer” (1 John 3:15). Esau’s silent vow already breaks the spirit of the sixth commandment.

Jacob is not blameless in the quarrel; his deceit gave Esau occasion for wrath. Yet a wrong suffered never licenses a wrong returned. “Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath: neither give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27). Esau made room for the adversary, and the struggle that began in the womb now threatens blood. The great controversy between good and evil runs through households as well as nations. Only God’s grace could turn this hatred into the embrace that would one day meet Jacob on the road home (33:4).

wordNotes.term: וַיִּשְׂטֹם (vayyistom) — and hated
wordNotes.explanation: The verb שָׂטַם (satam) means to bear a grudge or cherish animosity, hostility that persists and waits for its moment. Joseph’s brothers fear he will treat them this way after Jacob’s death, and Jacob’s blessing on Joseph recalls archers who “hated him.” It names settled resentment rather than a passing flash of anger.

wordNotes.term: יְמֵי אֵבֶל אָבִי (yeme ʾevel ʾavi) — the days of mourning for my father
wordNotes.explanation: אֵבֶל (ʾevel) is the formal period of grief observed after a death; Joseph kept seven days of mourning for Jacob, and Israel mourned Moses thirty days. Esau plans to respect that custom and then commit murder, a grim mixture of filial regard and hatred.

verses.bibleText: And these words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah: and she sent and called Jacob her younger son, and said unto him, Behold, thy brother Esau, as touching thee, doth comfort himself, purposing to kill thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And these words of Esau her elder son were told to Rebekah.” The plan Esau formed in his heart had evidently been spoken aloud to someone, and the report reached his mother. The household was less private than anyone supposed; in this family secrets keep escaping.

Rebekah acts at once. She sends for “Jacob her younger son” and tells him, “Behold, thy brother Esau, as touching thee, doth comfort himself, purposing to kill thee.” The narrator names both sons as hers, the elder and the younger. She loves both, and now the son she favored is in danger from the son she helped defraud. Her scheme has turned back on her own household.

“Doth comfort himself” is a striking phrase. Esau consoles himself for the lost blessing by planning revenge; the thought of Jacob’s death brings him relief. Revenge often works this way, a counterfeit comfort that soothes wounded pride while poisoning the heart. Scripture points the other way: “Recompense to no man evil for evil,” and “avenge not yourselves… for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord” (Romans 12:17, 19). The law had the same heart: “Thou shalt not avenge, nor bear any grudge” (Leviticus 19:18).

A servant’s report saved Jacob’s life. God’s care often works through ordinary channels, and the One who had chosen Jacob would not let Esau’s fury cut off the line of promise.

wordNotes.term: מִתְנַחֵם (mitnakhem) — doth comfort himself
wordNotes.explanation: The reflexive form of נָחַם (nakham), to be comforted or console oneself. Isaac “was comforted” after his mother’s death through his marriage to Rebekah, and Jacob later “refused to be comforted” over Joseph. Here Esau finds his consolation in planned bloodshed, a dark twist on a word usually tied to healing grief.

verses.bibleText: Now therefore, my son, obey my voice; and arise, flee thou to Laban my brother to Haran;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now therefore, my son, obey my voice; and arise, flee thou to Laban my brother to Haran.” For the third time Rebekah tells Jacob to obey her voice (compare vv. 8, 13). The first two commands drew him into deceit; this one sends him into exile. These are her last recorded words to her son.

Haran lay far to the north in upper Mesopotamia, where Abraham had lived before entering Canaan (11:31–12:4) and where Rebekah’s family remained. Abraham’s servant had once made the long journey there with ten camels and rich gifts to find a wife for Isaac (24:10). Jacob must go alone, as a fugitive. The verb “flee” marks the urgency: this is escape, not a planned visit.

Jacob will flee again when he leaves Laban (31:21), and Hosea remembers both journeys: “Jacob fled into the country of Syria, and Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he kept sheep” (Hosea 12:12). The man who grasped the blessing by cunning begins his life as heir of the promise with nothing in his hand but a staff (32:10). God often begins His work with His chosen through loss, so that the blessing will rest on grace rather than on possessions or schemes.

wordNotes.term: בְּרַח (berakh) — flee
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of בָּרַח (barakh), to flee or run away. It is used again when Jacob flees from Laban, and Hosea recalls that “Jacob fled into the country of Syria.” Both departures are hurried escapes, framing Jacob’s years in Haran between two flights.

verses.bibleText: And tarry with him a few days, until thy brother's fury turn away;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And tarry with him a few days, until thy brother’s fury turn away.” Rebekah expects a short absence. She believes Esau’s anger will cool soon and Jacob will be able to come home. In fact he would stay twenty years (31:41), and Genesis records no further meeting between mother and son.

The phrase “a few days” returns later with tender irony. Jacob served seven years for Rachel, “and they seemed unto him but a few days, for the love he had to her” (29:20). The words his mother used for a brief exile come to describe years of labor sweetened by love. Human plans measure time one way, and God’s purposes another. “Boast not thyself of to morrow; for thou knowest not what a day may bring forth” (Proverbs 27:1). James adds that life is a vapor, so believers should say, “If the Lord will” (James 4:14–15). Rebekah’s confident forecast shows how little any of them could see ahead.

wordNotes.term: יָמִים אֲחָדִים (yamim ʾakhadim) — a few days
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “some days,” an expression for a short, indefinite period. The same phrase describes Jacob’s seven years of service that “seemed unto him but a few days” because of his love for Rachel. Daniel uses it of a brief span after which a ruler falls.

verses.bibleText: Until thy brother's anger turn away from thee, and he forget that which thou hast done to him: then I will send, and fetch thee from thence: why should I be deprived also of you both in one day?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Rebekah goes on: “Until thy brother’s anger turn away from thee, and he forget that which thou hast done to him: then I will send, and fetch thee from thence.” Notice her phrase, “that which thou hast done to him.” She now speaks as though the deed were Jacob’s alone, though she had planned every step. Whether from tact or from self-protection, she lays the responsibility on her son.

Her promise, “I will send, and fetch thee,” was never kept. No message from her reaches Haran in the narrative, and when Jacob returns, he comes at the LORD’s command, not his mother’s (31:3). Even well-meant human plans cannot secure the future.

Her closing question lays bare her fear: “why should I be deprived also of you both in one day?” If Esau killed Jacob, she would lose Jacob to death and Esau to the penalty for murder, whether through an avenger of blood or through banishment like Cain’s (4:12–14; 9:6). The word “deprived” is the Hebrew term for bereavement, the loss of children. Rebekah sees that her scheme could cost her both sons at once.

In a sense her fear came true, though not by bloodshed. Jacob went away, and Esau drifted further from the family’s covenant life. The mother who sought to secure the blessing for her favorite lost the company of both sons. The cost of deceit is often counted in broken relationships. Yet God’s grace was larger than Rebekah’s failure. He would guard Jacob, prosper him, reconcile the brothers, and bring from Jacob’s line the One in whom “all the families of the earth” would be blessed (28:14).

wordNotes.term: אֶשְׁכַּל (ʾeshkal) — be deprived
wordNotes.explanation: From שָׁכֹל (shakhol), to be bereaved, especially of children. Jacob uses the same verb in his old age when he fears losing Benjamin: “If I be bereaved of my children, I am bereaved,” and when he laments, “Me have ye bereaved of my children.” Rebekah’s fear anticipates her son’s own sorrow.

verses.bibleText: And Rebekah said to Isaac, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth: if Jacob take a wife of the daughters of Heth, such as these which are of the daughters of the land, what good shall my life do me?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Rebekah said to Isaac, I am weary of my life because of the daughters of Heth.” Rebekah now turns to her husband, but she says nothing of Esau’s threat. She appeals instead to a grief they share: Esau’s Hittite wives, who had been “a grief of mind” to them both (26:34–35). She presents the journey to Haran as a search for a suitable wife rather than an escape.

The reason she gives is a real one. Marriage outside the covenant community endangered the family’s faith. Abraham had made his servant swear not to take a wife for Isaac from the Canaanites (24:3–4), and the concern was spiritual, not ethnic: Canaanite households served other gods, and their ways would draw the family away from the LORD. Paul applies the same principle to believers: “Be ye not unequally yoked together with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14).

Yet the way she makes her appeal shows how far honest speech has broken down in this marriage. She cannot speak plainly to her husband about what has happened or about Esau’s intent. She frames the request in terms that will win Isaac’s consent without reopening the wound. Perhaps she wished to spare him grief; perhaps she feared exposure. Either way, the household that began with prayer and clear divine guidance at the well (24:12–27, 63–67) now runs on managed information.

Her words, “what good shall my life do me?” are emotionally charged, perhaps heightened to move Isaac, and they succeed. In the next chapter Isaac calls Jacob, knowingly blesses him with the blessing of Abraham, and sends him to Padan-aram (28:1–5). The blessing once taken by stealth is now given openly. God brings good out of a tangle of human motives and keeps His promise even in a family as divided as this one.

wordNotes.term: קַצְתִּי בְחַיַּי (qatsti vekhayyay) — I am weary of my life
wordNotes.explanation: The verb קוּץ (quts) means to loathe or feel sick of something. Israel in the wilderness said, “our soul loatheth this light bread,” using a related expression. Rebekah’s phrase conveys intense distress over Esau’s marriages, which had already made life bitter for both parents.

wordNotes.term: בְּנוֹת חֵת (benot Khet) — daughters of Heth
wordNotes.explanation: The women of the Hittite clans living in Canaan, from whom Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah and Esau took his wives. Genesis reckons Heth among the descendants of Canaan, so the phrase stands for marriage outside the covenant family.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What happens in a family when each member tries to secure God’s promise by a private plan instead of trusting His word?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God’s declared purpose for Jacob stands in spite of the scheming of every member of the family, yet each one reaps sorrow from trying to accomplish God’s will by sinful means.
discussionQuestions: How does Isaac’s secret plan set the stage for Rebekah’s deception, and what does that teach about the influence of a spiritual leader’s choices?
Why does Jacob object only to the risk of being caught, and what does that reveal about his heart at this stage?
Why does Isaac say “yea, and he shall be blessed” instead of cursing Jacob or withdrawing his words?
What does Hebrews 12:16–17 teach about Esau’s tears, and how is that sorrow different from repentance?
Where do you see the consequences of the deception unfolding in the rest of Jacob’s story?
commonMisunderstandings: The success of the deception does not mean God approved it; the blessing reached Jacob because God had chosen him, and every participant paid heavily for the lie.
Isaac’s words were not a magic formula operating on their own; they stood because they agreed with the purpose God had already revealed.
Esau’s tears do not show God refusing a sincere penitent; he sought to reverse the outcome, not to forsake the attitude that had despised the birthright.
God’s choice of Jacob concerns the line of promise and its mission to the world, not an arbitrary decree fixing anyone’s eternal destiny.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Hold together God’s sovereign faithfulness and the honest record of human sin: the promise survives because God keeps it, while the deception costs Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Esau dearly.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Trust God to accomplish what He has promised, refuse the shortcuts that require deceit, and value His gifts now, while they are freely offered.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God’s blessing is a gift of grace received by faith; it cannot be seized by fraud or earned by service, and in Christ, the Seed of Abraham, it is offered openly to all.
flow: God promised the blessing of Abraham to Jacob before he was born.
Isaac, Rebekah, and Jacob each tried to control the outcome by their own plans, and deceit tore the family apart.
Esau, who had despised the birthright, wept for the blessing too late.
Christ bore the curse so that the blessing of Abraham might come to all who believe.
We receive that blessing openly by faith, without disguise, and we must not put off receiving it.
simpleIllustrations: A child who sneaks a gift from under the tree the night before receives what the parent meant to give anyway, but spoils the joy and trust of the giving.
Borrowed clothes may fool a blind man for a moment; a robe given by the King and worn openly needs no pretending.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop trying to secure God’s favor by your own schemes and receive the blessing He offers you freely in Christ today?
cautions: Do not present Jacob’s deceit as a model of faith; the narrative records it honestly as sin that God overruled.
Avoid treating Esau as beyond God’s compassion; Scripture warns through him while still showing God’s care for his descendants.
Do not turn Jacob’s disguise into an allegory of salvation; the contrast with the gospel is clearer than any likeness.

reflectionQuestions: Where am I tempted to help God fulfill His promises by methods He has forbidden?
Do I fear being found out more than I fear doing wrong?
Are there gifts from God that I am treating lightly now and may long for later?
Is there favoritism or secrecy in my relationships that is breeding mistrust?
Whom do I need to forgive, or seek forgiveness from, before resentment hardens into hatred?
